To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PGI2 stimulates BKCa channels in retinal microvascular pericytes via a cAMP-dependent, cross-activation pathway involving protein kinase G (PKG).

prostacyclin is a potent stimulant of BKCa channel in pericytes and this effect is mediated by cross-activation of protein kinase G. Burgoyne, Timothy, "Prostacyclin Stimulates Potassium Channel Activity in Porcine Retinal Pericytes via cAMP-Stimulated Cross-Activation of PKG" (2005).
PGI2 opens potassium channels by cyclic AMP-stimulation of cross-activation of the cGK (PKG) in retinal periclytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms of how PGI2 regulates retinal pericytic function and retinal vascular tone.
understanding the molecular basis for the regulation of retinal blood vessels.
understanding how PGI2 stimulates potassium channel activity, and thereby pericyte relaxation, in the retinal microvasculature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

prostacyclin (the most abundant prostanoids in the retinal microvasculature) is a potent stimulant of BKCa channel (large-conductance, calcium- and voltage-dependent) activity in retinal microvascular pericytes.
prostacyclin (the major endogenous vasodilator in the retina) stimulates potassium channels (BKCa) in retinal pericyles via a cAMP-dependent, cross-activation pathway of PKG.
the PGI2-induced increase in BKCa activity in pericytes is mediated by PKA-stimulated cross activation of PKG.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

prostacyclin stimulates the activity of large-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ channels in retinal microvascular pericytes by a cyclic AMP-stimultated, cross-activation pathway involving the cGMP-activated protein kinase.

prostacyclin is a potent stimulatory agent for retinal pericytic BKCa channel activity, and that this response is mediated, at least in-part, by cAMP-stimulating, cross-activation (i.e., phosphorylation) of PKG, rather than PKA.
prostacyclin (a vasodilator in the retina) is a potent stimulant of BKCa channels in retinal microvascular pericytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
prostacyclin (the most abundant vasodilator in the retina) stimulates the activity of a potassium channel, BKCa, in retinal periclytes.

prostacyclin is a very potent stimulator of the large conductance, voltage and calcium-activated K+ channel (BKCa) in retinal pericites, and this effect is mediated by a cAMP-stimuted cross-activation of the cGPM-dependent protein kinase.
prostacyclin (a prostanoid) is a potent stimulant of BKCa channel in retinal pericites, and this response is mediated by cAMP-dependent activation of the cGPK.
